'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.
  • In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
  • In a recent development, "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

In a recent development, "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she notes. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life.".

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Recent findings suggest that since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

It has been revealed that they gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Industry observers note that some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

Recent findings suggest that "Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," claims Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous.".

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she indicates.

Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade.

Sources indicate that war is not upcoming to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

It has been revealed that houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

Industry observers note that more than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

Recent findings suggest that in recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he notes. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him.".

Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", notes Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor notes.

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," states Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he claims. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents.".

We have not been able to independently verify these figures.

He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he states.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

In a recent development, he tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

In a recent development, the Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He notes the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

According to recent reports, "Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

How long can the city hold out, I ask.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

In a recent development, akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

Sources indicate that when Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Recent findings suggest that last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (Â£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

It has been revealed that "This time the Houthis have latest technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves.".

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is at the moment designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

Recent findings suggest that "They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city.".

Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months.

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

According to recent reports, "Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes.".

According to recent reports, the people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he indicates, "because we don't see any move to help us.".

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

But could they fight their way in?

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party.".

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

Industry observers note that "Please don't forget Taiz," she indicates. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports.".

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor.

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • PM challenges rivals to rebuff proposal he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope.
  • Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack.
  • Sources indicate that this is undoubtedly true.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PM challenges rivals to rebuff proposal he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope.

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The notable point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he remarked. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”.

Sources indicate that this is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a fresh youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

Industry observers note that but as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”.

For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.

It has been revealed that to begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A newly introduced constituency-level survey released on Friday highlighted that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

Recent findings suggest that they, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he mentioned, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he remarked, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

In a recent development, kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.

More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.

While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.

Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).
  • According to recent reports, more than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.
  • It has been revealed that the Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).

According to recent reports, more than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.

It has been revealed that the Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.

“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.

Sources indicate that microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the tech giant.

“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard notes.

According to recent reports, howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”.

The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes indicates the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.

Howes indicates that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.

Leard notes that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI.

The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.).

Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.

“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”.

Enhancement: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.

Latest Update: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request.
  • In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.
  • Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request.

In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also stated: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most key matter of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”.

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to complications surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order asserts that the translation complications cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

Recent findings suggest that the Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.

The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”.

The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, remarked: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”.

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

According to recent reports, “It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.

“This [extradition case] demonstrates the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.
  • Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's upcoming political generation and its giant neighbour.
  • It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's upcoming political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of problems, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

Nepal suffered devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands missing.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Massive Brother' attitude of Delhi.

Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The newly introduced Nepali leadership notes they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

According to recent reports, "They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

India and Nepal share an open border and longstanding economic ties.

One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

According to recent reports, "India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.

India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

Sources indicate that in 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

According to recent reports, "I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border matter with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

According to recent reports, while Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army declared Thursday that it would delay a strategy to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air.
  • The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs).
  • “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle stated in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army declared Thursday that it would delay a strategy to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle stated in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

Telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

Industry observers note that lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army said. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

Recent findings suggest that in an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army said that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

According to recent reports, the military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it said the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

According to recent reports, in all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” plan the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army said the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the strategy is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

According to recent reports, the Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

Modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

Sources indicate that during the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

The Army’s initiative was to communicate clearly with the public about the prepares, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

In its environmental risk assessment, the Army said it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the strategy.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the strategy “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting aims until it can review the case.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras.

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they remarked was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

Recent findings suggest that the officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Recent findings suggest that zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

In a recent development, zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He noted the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

It has been revealed that the three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

According to recent reports, the officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.

The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.

Recent findings suggest that she said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”.

The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Industry observers note that zecler’s lawyers and supporters remarked the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an vital moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”.

He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”.

Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”.

Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.

Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated.

A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One states 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.".

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting.

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

It has been revealed that now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

A string of grisly discoveries in the suburbs near Manila has put thousands of grieving pet owners on edge.

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

According to recent reports, on 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

It has been revealed that chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting â taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know.".

In a recent development, in the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

According to recent reports, "The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

Chris Taylor, pictured here with a dog unrelated to the scandal, has uncovered the remains of some 170 dead pets in recent weeks.

Industry observers note that by crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris indicates. "Others were liquefied.".

According to recent reports, LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

It has been revealed that their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Industry observers note that some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

It has been revealed that as more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

According to recent reports, "So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," indicates Chris. "And man, it just flooded in.".

Ahjay Paws, the company that was supposed to cremate Olaf, is under investigation.

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

According to recent reports, A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," claims Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets.".

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Pet care - including for those that have died - has become a booming industry in the Philippines.

According to recent reports, revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, claims she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (Â£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling states Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

In a recent development, "Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she indicates. "We need to know what happened.".

Pets have been found dumped in bags like this - with labels giving their names and weights.

In a recent development, earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT â but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law â estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them â and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

In a recent development, two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The firm is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

Sources indicate that the BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm mentioned the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

The pet-dumping scandal, in which Olaf may have been a victim, has blown up into a national controversy.

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, indicates she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (Â£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she indicates. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his.".

Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns.".

Industry observers note that in response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

On 2 November, Percival Vilar CendaÃ±a of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations.".

It has been revealed that neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real â and CendaÃ±a was giving voice to a common sentiment.

"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he stated.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.

But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.

Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".

Recent findings suggest that the scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like CendaÃ±a are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.

Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.

Chris Taylor dealing with items resembling clothing found at a dumpsite (blurred at source).

One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".

"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she noted.

Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he claims.

According to recent reports, "They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them.".

As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he notes.

The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr mentioned authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.

"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez remarked.

"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families.".

Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.

Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.

"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," claims Calling.â¯ "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever.".

Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated.".

She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days.".

With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA+ adds a few perks to GTA 6 and one of them is already stirring up players.
  • A lot has changed in gaming in the 13 years since Grand Theft Auto 5 debuted.
  • That $8 gets you a few perks in GTA 6, but nothing game-changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA+ adds a few perks to GTA 6 and one of them is already stirring up players.

A lot has changed in gaming in the 13 years since Grand Theft Auto 5 debuted. That includes the explosion of live-service games and gaming subscriptions, and the Grand Theft Auto franchise has gotten in on both with GTA Online and the GTA+ membership. Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is out, GTA+ members get some additional benefits in the upcoming game on top of what the subscription already offers in GTA Online.

That $8 gets you a few perks in GTA 6, but nothing game-changing. You'll get 10 percent more money for any eligible vehicles you sell in the game and a 10 percent discount at a variety of stores. You can also use in-game transport options like scooters, bikes and public transit for free and get a premium membership to the RydeMe rideshare service. Together, those perks add up to a few cheaper ways to get around GTA 6's huge map and an easier time making cash. That can make a significant difference in your progress early in the game, since cheats don't unlock until you beat the story.

Sources indicate that the biggest and most controversial benefit is one you can claim only after reaching GTA 6's third chapter. At that point, you'll get the '90 Annis Venturas BLVD Elegy, a free sports car, plus a garage in the Crosstown area. Locking exclusive items in a single-player game behind a monthly subscription is never popular, and players have already voiced their displeasure on Reddit.

For most players, the GTA+ subscription fee probably isn't worth it for what it adds to GTA 6 alone. From the start, GTA+ has focused mostly on GTA Online, giving members in-game currency and discounts, latest vehicles and garages to store them in, and a rotating suite of items and features. For dedicated GTA Online players who also picked up GTA 6, there's a much better case for the subscription.

The game library included with GTA+ might make it worth it for more people. Anyone with an active subscription also gets access to a selection of Rockstar's other games, including Red Dead Redemption and GTA 5. Of course, you might not have time for any of those until you finish a campaign that can run 80 hours, but the library does make the $8 subscription much easier to justify.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple challenges” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

Sources indicate that while Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

Sources indicate that according to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The Fresh York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center manufacturer named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

Industry observers note that after the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view complications of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”.

“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person stated.

Industry observers note that in recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has mentioned played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

Sources indicate that board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis.

Sources indicate that already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the organization’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls.

Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board.

In the firm’s all-hands meeting on November 18, board chair Jones noted it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.”.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk, have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has noted he would be “honored” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a major apology.”.

The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return.

Some employees are miffed at how promptly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” says one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.”.

Industry observers note that at the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress mentioned employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him.

Industry observers note that “The ship has sinked but there’s no plan to be transparent about what happened,” says one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”.

#12819. Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
